Breeze of Breslov

Parshat Chayei Sarah | Oct. 29-30, 2021

“Like a Phoenix”

By Rabbi David Yisrael Kalmus

(Dedicated to my two grandmothers who were niftar this past year, Sarah Esther bat Yaakov and Tzippora bat Yitzhak)

Rebbe Nachman’s main disciple, Rav Natan, wrote a phenomenal biography about his Rebbe titled, “Chayeh Moharan”, “The Life of our Master and Teacher, Nachman”. Rav Natan also wrote a raw and often vulnerable autobiography about himself titled “Yemot Moranat”, “The Days of our Master and Teacher, Natan”.

In explaining why Rav Natan used the term “Life” when dealing with his Rebbe, and “Days” when referring to himself, Rav Natan stated that all of his days joined together to produce one full life. But as for Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, every single day he had brand new life!

This constant, genuine renewal of life force for Rebbe Nachman was something wondrous and often inexplicable. However, Rebbe Nachman himself teaches the secret of his daily, Phoenix-like renewal.

In Likutey Moharan, Rebbe Nachman states that the one common feature of all spiritual masters is that the only moment that exists for them is right now. They never ruminate about yesterday or contemplate tomorrow.

Instead, they throw themselves into the present moment with “all their heart, all their soul, and all their might”, as if it’s the only moment that has or will ever exist.

In this week’s Parsha, “Chayeh Sarah”, we learn about the unique life and passing of our foremother Sarah. Interestingly, the Torah states that she lived “100 years, and 20 years, and 7 years. These were the life of Sarah.”

All the Sages are busy trying to find the reason for the bizarre and seemingly unnecessary breakdown of the years of her life. Just say she lived until 127 years old and be done with it. “Yallah”, as my wife would say.

The Sages conclude that the Torah is highlighting that in every period of Sarah’s lifetime, she was truly alive. In this way, Sarah life was remarkable.

You might wrongly assume then that the life of Sarah must have been one of great grandeur and splendor. The truth is that Sarah’s life, like that of all the Tzaddikim, was often one of tremendous hardship and heartbreak.

Sarah was abducted and threatened to be molested on two separate occasions, not knowing if she would be saved from her scary predicament. Sarah’s one true aspiration was to have children, and yet this was the very thing she struggled with her whole life. As a result, Sarah had to standby and watch as her husband consorted with their maidservant, having a child together a full decade before Sarah had hers. The maidservant taunted Sarah regarding this predicament, leaving her frustrated and demoralized. Sarah’s life concluded when she faced the immanent death of her one son Yitzhak.

Yet with all of this, Sarah is the only person in the entire Torah to have a Parsha dedicated to the greatness of her life. Not Môshè Rabbeinu. Not David HaMelech. Not even Sarah’s husband Avraham Avinu. Only Sarah life was called “Life”.

The vital lesson we learn from this is that success in this world has nothing to do with being successful. The quality of ones life isn’t defined by the events that take place or the achievements one experiences. Instead, “The Tzaddik falls seven times and gets back up”. It is one’s resilience and refusal to stay down forever that serves as their true barometer for greatness. In this measure, Sarah was alive. In this measure. Rebbe Nachman was alive. And in this measure, we can all achieve true life as well.

May H” bless us with the courage and wisdom to understand that real success doesn’t preclude falling. Only that in the end, we get back up.

Like a Phoenix.

Like a Tzaddik.

Like Sarah.

Shabbat Shalom.

Selecting a Spouse

By Rabbi Benyamin Vineburg

Many of our readers, myself included, are or have recently been involved in shidduchim or dating relationships. The process of finding and selecting a soulmate is arduous, time consuming, vulnerable and, frankly, expensive. It takes a great deal of commitment and Emunah to do one’s due diligence, check references, travel for dates and be open and vulnerable a little more than usual.

This process, whether religious or secular, has become all the more difficult in a world where on-demand “feel goods” have replaced the need or desire for communication, understanding or hard work. In the United States, the divorce rates nears nearly 50%, not because we don’t have means to communicate or build relationships; social media has certainly taken care of that; but because we choose not to.

In this week’s parsha, Eliezer is sent by Avraham to find a wife for Yitzchak. Like any good Jewish parent, Avraham made sure to give Eliezer very specific requirements as to whom would be a suitable match. Eliezer is shown by Hashem a sign that Rivka, due to her kindness towards his animals and then him at the water well, is the right choice for Yitzchak.

I know what you’re thinking. I have asked Hashem for a sign for my own significant other too…where is my sign at the well? Perhaps Rivka’s actions can give us an answer.

Rivka embodied two incredible qualities; kindness and modesty. Many rabbaim and shadchanim remind us frequently of the importance of finding a baalat chesed and a tzinuah. She withdrew her external qualities in order to fully give of her internal qualities and it is those internal qualities that ultimately “got her the job.”

Many of us may be waiting for our sign at the well but we aren’t committed to looking at our perspective matches with the proper lens. I cannot count how many times I’ve had friends or students tell me that they refuse dates because of “their height”, “their body shape”, or “their upbringing.” Many dates are over before they’ve started because we have this twisted notion that our partner will resemble that of Johnny Depp or Angelina Jolie; and care very little for the substantive, realness of those we meet.

Rivka embodied qualities that we all can use to find our proper partners. She was kind and humble; giving first for giving sake and expecting nothing in return. She was modest, unpretentious and real; a quality that bodes well for a communicative and honest partner who will always seek to uplift rather than break down. She was calm and slow to anger; she had middot tovot, a solid foundation and grasp for who she was. These are the qualities to look for in a partner.

This week, exemplify the middot of Rivka. Give for giving’s sake. Be humble and modest. Look for the good in yourself and others. Have Emunah that Hashem will focus light upon you as you focus your light on others. Ask Hashem to give you a new or existing relationship with the qualities of Rivka, then, I pray, may you receive your sign and miracle speedily.

Good Shabbos.

By Aaron London, RN

My dear friends, I would like to share words of Torah with you this week that might be heavier than in past weeks.

In the days between the 12th and 16th of Tishrei, the Piaseczno Rebbe lost his son, his son’s wife, and his sister-in-law to the horrific Nazi air assults of September 1939. The Rebbe, who had begun to share divrei chizuk on Shabbos with his chasidim and anyone who was willing to listen, entered into a six-week silence (Abramson 78).

Then, on the Shabbos of November 4th, Parshas Chayei Sarah, the Rebbe spoke.

The Rebbe references a teaching found in sefer Ma’or va-Shemesh in the name of R’ Menacham Mendel of Rimanov. The Gemara in Brachos (5a) explains, “A covenant is made with salt, and a covenant is made with afflictions. Just as salt makes meat palatable, so too afflictions purify the individual of sins. The Ma’or va-Shemesh in the name of R’ Menacham Mendel of Rimanov comments, “Just as one cannot derive pleasure from meat that has been excessively salted, rather only if it was properly salted, so too afflictions should be meted out only in such measure that they can be tolerated, and with an admixture of mercy” (translation from R’ Henry Abramson’s Torah from the Years of Wrath, 80).

The Rebbe, utilizing the teaching of his great-grandfather, perceives a haunting chiddush in the Torah’s placement of Sarah’s death next to the Akeidas Yitzchak. Rashi comments, “the death of Sarah was juxtaposed to the binding of Yitzchak because with the news that her son was being bound and was about to be sacrificed, her soul burst forth from her and she died” (Bereshis 23:2). The Rebbe then explains that this juxtaposition was “in order to advocate for us, indicating what results from excessive afflictions, Heaven forbid – her soul burst forth” (80).

In his comments on this piece from the sefer Aish Kodesh, R’ Moshe Weinberger remarks that Sarah died form the horror of what might have been. She was broken from the unpredictability of life, of the uncertainty of each moment.

R’ Henry Abramson, in his work Torah from the Years of Wrath, which offers historical context in understanding the Torahs from sefer Aish Kodesh, comments, “It is difficult not to read an autobiographical perspective in this sermon – was the Rebbe not expressing a tiny part of his own ineffable anguish” (83)?

Indeed, as the Rebbe remarks, if Sarah Aminu who was a tzeddekas on the highest level, died out of the possibility of horror, what of us (the Rebbe ultimately explains that Sarah sacrificed herself for the Jewish people in order to convey to Hashem so-to-speak that the suffering was too much to bear)?

In the work I do with people who suffer from addiction, I often encounter those who have experienced some of the most unspeakable trauma. Sometimes, in a playful moment with my own daughter, my heart stops and I drift into a space where the residual energy of my patients surfaces to my mind and I shudder – what if… what if…. (lo aleinu).

There is the possibility of horror and horror itself and the trauma we all encounter in various degrees and intensities. How can we coexist with these two paradoxical notions – on the one hand the moment is uncertain and on the other hand, Hashem is lovingly guiding us through these very same moments to our ultimate tachlis? What happens when the moment is too much for us to bear?

My dear friends, it is here I tread on such delicate ground.

We engage with emunah at various ways. I can conceptually understand that everything Hashem does is for the good and for my ultimate benefit, but not feel that emunah within my emotional world. And, in the space inbetween my intellectual knowing and my emotional not-knowing, I encounter all the different expressions of inner turbulence.

R’ Joey Rosenfeld in the name of Rebbe Nachman and our tzaddikim will often mention the concept in his shiurim that the tachlis of knowing is not knowing, that the highest point of knowledge is for a person to ultimately admit that he does not and cannot truly know the essence of Hashem’s conduct. Perhaps, perched at the edge of a person’s conceptual recognition that everything emanates from Hashem, he then allows himself to fall into the vulnerability of not knowing. And, in his willingness to proclaim that he cannot understand the essence of why Hashem is doing this or that, he paradoxically allows his emotional world to fill with the simple emunah that Hashem is truly in control. A person, in his admittance, then says, “Hashem, I do not know. The moment is uncertain. And I am okay with not knowing.”

In truth, it is precisely through our ability to make a space for uncertainty that we offer ourselves the gift of okayness. I no longer have to resist the moment even though the moment is difficult or uncomfortable. Or, as I have heard R’ Rosenfeld mention, I can be okay even when things are not okay.

When we have the courage to be okay, we then open ourselves up to the possibility of redemption that lives within every moment.

Gut Shabbos,

A.L.Y
